content.title: He ordered genocide in Bosnia-Herzegovina: War criminal Ratko Mladic dies
content.lead: Mladic said he became an officer to protect Yugoslavia and all its peoples before the war. Afterward, he became the primary perpetrator of the genocide. Some still revere him.
content.author: Andreas Ernst

image.author: Radivoje Pavicic / AP
image.caption: General Ratko Mladic in September 1994 with soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska.
image.altText: FILE - Bosnian Serb General Ratko Mladic speaks to soldiers near the Bosnian town of Cazin, Sept. 4, 1994. (AP Photo/Radivoje Pavicic, File) Ratko Mladic

content.caption: General Ratko Mladic in September 1994 with soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska.
content.author: Radivoje Pavicic / AP

content.text: The public last heard from Ratko Mladic nine years ago. In November 2017, the key figure responsible for the Srebrenica genocide was convicted by the Hague war crimes tribunal. Afterward, Mladic faded from Western consciousness. In the former Yugoslav countries, he became a ghost, a symbol of Serbian ultranationalism.

His image is sprayed on house walls in Belgrade by provocateurs and then painted over by activists. A few days later, it reappears. Most of these young people didn't even know if he was still alive. Now Ratko Mladic is dead. He died in prison on Thursday at the age of 84.

During the trial in The Hague, the former general was severely impaired mentally and physically. During the sentencing, he began to curse loudly. The judge had rejected the request to shorten the hearing due to the accused's poor health. Mladic was led out of the courtroom. The proceedings continued.

The final verdict, life imprisonment, was based on extensive evidence. The court found that Mladic had been involved in four «joint criminal enterprises»: the expulsion of Bosniaks and Croats from various areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina; the terrorization of the encircled, besieged city of Sarajevo (1991–1995); the murder of thousands of men and boys near Srebrenica in 1995; and the hostage-taking of UN personnel in the same year.

image.author: Reuters
image.caption: Mentally and physically affected: Mladic in court in The Hague.
image.altText: Ratko Mladic in The Hague on Wednesday. Reuters

content.caption: Mentally and physically affected: Mladic in court in The Hague.
content.author: Reuters

content.text: The massacres were not simply the result of brutalization by war. They were based on a plan, largely devised by Radovan Karadzic, the political leader of the Bosnian Serbs. On May 12, 1992, General Mladic appeared in the parliament of the Bosnian Serbs.

When politicians confronted him with their intention to create an ethnically «pure» territory, Mladic said: «We cannot cleanse; we do not have a sieve so that the Serbs remain and the others leave. That is not possible. ... People, this is genocide!» Two weeks later, he shed his inhibitions. During the shelling of Sarajevo, Mladic ordered: «Aim at Velesici, aim at Pofalici, there are only a few Serbs there.»

Hatred of other ethnic groups was not ingrained in Mladic from birth. He was born in 1943 into a partisan family in eastern Bosnia. His father died in one of the last battles of the war. Mladic embarked on a military career and built a brilliant career in the Yugoslav People's Army.

In 1991, as the country disintegrated, he was sent to Croatia. «I serve Yugoslavia,» he said at the time. He said the army had to protect all nations and minorities in the country. Shortly thereafter, the war spread to Bosnia, and Mladic became Chief of Staff of the VRS, the newly formed Army of Republika Srpska.

The first indictment by the Hague Tribunal was issued in 1995, shortly after the mass murders near Srebrenica. This initially bothered Mladic little. After the war, he fled to Serbia and moved around Belgrade as a free man – albeit under heavy guard. When the deposed Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic was extradited to The Hague by reform politician Zoran Djindjic in 2001, Mladic went into hiding. But only partially. Within the intelligence service and the army, he still had a large, reliable network that protected and financed him.

His helpers came under pressure only in 2006, after the EU had linked any rapprochement between Serbia and cooperation with The Hague. Increasingly dependent on family and close friends, Mladic's situation gradually became difficult. Nevertheless, it would take until 2011 for him to be tracked down and arrested in the house of a relative in northern Serbia.

image.author: AP
image.caption: Mladic with Dutch Colonel Thom Karremans in July 1995 in Potocari. The passivity of the UN peacekeeping forces enabled the genocide in Srebrenica.
image.altText: Bosnian Serb army General Ratko Mladic, left, drinks with Dutch military Col. Ton Karremans, second right, in the village of Potocari, in this July 12, 1995 photo. Using an impressive collection of archive footage, Leslie Woodhead recounts the events at Srebrenica in the film 'A Cry From the Grave' at the annual International Documentary Film Festival in Amsterdam, Monday, November 29, 1999, The Netherlands. Among some of the most interesting footage is a Serb military recording where a frightened and Timid Karremans is seen virtually pleading for the life of his troops during negotiations with Gen. Mladic. (KEYSTONE/AP PHOTO/STR) === ===

content.caption: Mladic with Dutch Colonel Thom Karremans in July 1995 in Potocari. The passivity of the UN peacekeeping forces enabled the genocide in Srebrenica.
content.author: AP

content.text: Criminal proceedings were initially launched against eleven of his escape helpers in Serbia. All but one were later acquitted. The indictment remained sealed, reportedly because it could harm the «reputation of the country.» This is a clear indication that Mladic was not only protected by the «deep state» but also by high-ranking politicians for a long time.

Although hardly anyone today denies that serious crimes were committed in Srebrenica in the name of the Serbian people, politicians and the majority of the public continue to dispute that the events constituted genocide. The silence surrounding the crime was not continuous. In 2005, a video briefly shook the country. The film shows how Serbian paramilitaries near Srebrenica abuse, mock, and then cold-bloodedly shoot a group of adolescent boys. A debate tentatively began. But it soon died down again.

In people's daily lives, the war that ended thirty years ago no longer plays a significant role. Only the elderly can personally remember the grim 1990s. Nor are the Balkans any longer home to Europe's most successful and dangerous nationalists. But the fact that Ratko Mladic continues to exist as a symbol on walls and in football chants indicates that the Serbian public has not yet detoxified itself.

image.author: Dado Ruvic / Reuters
image.caption: A Bosniak mother at the graves of her two sons, who were killed by Mladic's troops in July 1995.
image.altText: Mejra Dzogaz touches the graves of her two sons before the television broadcast of the court proceedings of former Bosnian Serb general Ratko Mladic's in Potocari, near Srebrenica, May 17, 2012. Mejra's husband, three sons and a grandson were killed during the Srebrenica massacre in 1995 by a Serbian army unit commanded by Mladic. The Bosnian Serb general made a throat-slitting gesture to a woman who lost her son, husband and brothers in the Srebenica massacre at the start of his trial on Wednesday for some of the worst atrocities in Europe since World War Two. REUTERS/Dado Ruvic (BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA - Tags: POLITICS CONFLICT CRIME LAW)

metadata.nzzSummaryEN:
- Former Bosnian Serb military leader Ratko Mladic has died at the age of 84 in The Hague.
- He was sentenced to life imprisonment in 2017 for genocide and other war crimes; his health had recently deteriorated.
- An official confirmation of his death by the UN mechanism is still pending.
metadata.nzzSummaryDE:
- Former Bosnian Serb military chief Ratko Mladic has died in The Hague at the age of 84.
 - He was sentenced to life imprisonment in 2017 for genocide and other war crimes; his health had recently deteriorated.
 - There has been no official confirmation of the death by the UN mechanism yet.
